posts.caption: In 2021, one engineer typed one wrong command and 3.5 billion people lost the internet in a single instant. Not hacked. Not attacked. Just one wrong line of code during a routine maintenance check. Facebook's own engineers couldn't even log in to fix it, their access tools were on the same servers that just vanished. They had to physically drive to data centers and override servers by hand. One by one. 6 hours. $60 million lost every single hour. And the exact same vulnerability? Still exists right now. The internet is more fragile than you think.

2021 mein ek engineer ne ek galat command type ki aur 3.5 billion logon ka internet ek pal mein band ho gaya. Hack nahi hua. Attack nahi hua. Bas ek routine maintenance check ke dauran ek galat line of code. 6 ghante. Har ghante 60 million dollar ka nuksaan. Internet utna strong nahi jitna hum sochte hain.

There is a sound that only 2% of people can hear. Scientists have studied it for 50 years and still have no answer. It's called The Hum — and the leading theory is that it's the Earth itself vibrating at a frequency most humans aren't built to detect. A woman heard it for 11 years, moved across the country to escape it, and it followed her to the new house. Stop right now, close your eyes, and listen. What do you hear?

We call space the final frontier. But we've barely explored our own planet. Earth is stranger than anything we've found out there — and most people have no idea. From perfect solar eclipses to oceans deeper than mountains are tall, this is the planet you thought you knew.

In 1974, a man calculated the exact day he would die and spent a year preparing for it. What happened next is stranger than the prediction itself. Frank was obsessed with numerology. He told his family, quit his job, and gave away everything he owned. When the day came and went without incident, he thought he'd beaten fate. He hadn't.

Death isn't a single switch that shuts down your entire body at once. When your heart stops beating and your brain goes silent, trillions of cells inside you are still alive, desperately trying to keep themselves running. Death isn't a single moment, but a slow and surprisingly complex process that can last for weeks.

What actually happens when you die? What makes death so mysterious, and which cells are the last survivors within your body? Watch our full video to find out!

recentPosts.caption:
At first glance, this peregrine falcon looks like he’s asking for silence. He’s in fact, taking a moment on the cliffside to clean his talons, an important part of keeping them ready for the hunt.⁠
⁠
Peregrine falcons are famous for their speed. In a hunting dive, they can reach over 200 miles per hour, which makes them widely known as the fastest animal on Earth.⁠
⁠
By: @scottsessionsphoto

Talk about travelling in style! 🌊🐌 An emperor shrimp catches a free ride on the Spanish dancer, one of the ocean’s largest sea slugs, growing up to 15 inches long. Named for its graceful, flamenco-like movements, this underwater beauty makes quite the ride for its tiny passenger. 🦐✨⁠
⁠
🎥: @scuba_moment

Tuscany looks incredible from above at sunrise. ⁠
⁠
@gabornagy_photography captured these aerial views of the Tuscan countryside in autumn, when the first light of day brings out the region’s rolling hills, winding gravel roads, and warm colors.⁠
⁠
To get these shots, he rode his road bike for 50 km along the famous Strade Bianche gravel roads in complete darkness, carrying his drone on his back to reach the perfect spots before sunrise.⁠
⁠
These photos were captured in October 2017.

A hike that feels almost unreal! ⛰️ ⁠
Harihar Fort in Maharashtra, India, sits at around 3,676 feet and is famous for its steep, narrow rock-cut steps that make the climb an unforgettable adventure. ⁠
⁠
Not for the faint-hearted, but what a view from the top! 😮⁠
🎥: @jithu_chandranc

Fly Geyser in Nevada looks like something from another planet, but it was actually created by accident.⁠
⁠
In the 1960s, a well was drilled here to search for geothermal energy and was never properly sealed. Hot water has been bursting out ever since, building up these strange mounds over the years. The bright colors come from tiny heat-loving algae that thrive in the warm, wet surface.⁠
⁠
Today, it sits on private land in the Black Rock Desert, and visitors can only see it up close on guided to

When it comes to impressing a potential mate, practice makes perfect! 🐦✨ ⁠
The Western Parotia, a bird of paradise native to the cloud forests of Indonesian Papua, clears a little stage in the forest and rehearses his elaborate courtship dance. ⁠
⁠
With ballerina-like moves, a shimmering blue and gold chest and six elegant head wires, he makes quite the performer.⁠
🎥: @andrew_clough_photography

Northern right whale dolphins are one of the few dolphin species without a dorsal fin, giving them a smooth, whale-like appearance. They can reach speeds of over 22 mph and are known for their impressive leaps and jumps.⁠
⁠
This pod of around 500 dolphins was spotted near California’s Northern Channel Islands, where they swam alongside the boat and rode its bow.⁠
⁠
Had you ever seen a dolphin without a dorsal fin? ⁠
⁠
By: @nathoutsidethebox

With its square face and serious stare, the Tibetan fox looks almost like a cartoon. ⁠
⁠
Its unusual head shape comes from thick fur and strong jaw muscles, which help it hunt pikas in the windy highlands of the Tibetan Plateau.⁠
⁠
These foxes live at elevations of up to about 17,000 feet. They’re sometimes seen following brown bears as they dig for pikas, waiting to grab any that escape.⁠
⁠⁠
What do you think this fox is thinking? 🤔⁠
⁠
By: @giovannini_jonathan

A traditional Konkan take on pasta! 🍝 ⁠
This local preparation turns simple ingredients into a dish with a familiar look but its own unique taste and cooking tradition.⁠
⁠
 A little reminder that every region has its own delicious way of doing things.⁠
🎥: @shravani10_

Most people see Antelope Canyon in the middle of the day, surrounded by tour groups. But after sunset, it’s possible to explore it on a guided night tour, with no crowds and only the stars above.⁠
⁠
These tours also let visitors learn about Navajo culture directly from the people who call this land home.⁠
⁠
Would you explore a slot canyon at night? ⁠
⁠
By: @clanger_mcbanger, with guide @nybimages

From yak milk to one of the hardest cheeses in the world. 🧀🐃⁠
Meet Chhurpi, a traditional Himalayan cheese made through a slow, hands-on process that turns yak milk into an incredibly firm delicacy. ⁠
⁠
And alongside it, freshly prepared yak butter, a taste of everyday life in the mountain communities of Sikkim.⁠
A little glimpse into food traditions that have stood the test of time. 🤍⁠
🎥: @utb_sikkim

On just a few winter evenings each year, the village of Shirakawa-go in Japan glows under the snow.⁠
⁠
Famous for its thatched-roof farmhouses, built with steep roofs to help heavy snow slide off, this UNESCO World Heritage village is lit up for a handful of nights in January and February. The event is so popular that visitors need to book in advance, as there are no same-day tickets ❄️⁠
⁠
Would you travel to Japan in winter to see this?⁠
⁠
By: @dongnejjicsa

Indris are the largest lemur species in the world, and they are known for their astonishingly loud, musical singing. Found in Madagascar, indris are among the many animals unique to the island—but their habitat is threatened. Now, to estimate the population, scientists are using a process known as passive acoustic monitoring to map the density and abundance of the endemic species.

Learn more about the efforts to protect indris at the link in bio. 

Video by Ethology Lab at the University of Tur

The extreme temperatures of a hydrothermal vent may not seem ideal for life, but a host of organisms can be found in this mineral-rich environment—and, for the first time, scientists have observed Antarctic krill among them.

This was part of the National Geographic and Rolex Perpetual Planet Southern Ocean Expedition conducted in collaboration with the Schmidt Ocean Institute aboard their research vessel Falkor (too).

The ketogenic diet has helped some people find relief from chronic migraines, but its restrictive nature and potential health risks make it a controversial treatment. Now, researchers are looking more closely at how rapid swings in blood sugar, which standard tests may miss, could play a role. While some patients respond better to the diet than others, experts hope their findings could lead to more personalized treatment options.

Learn more at the link in bio.

Illustration by NGM Staff; Photog

In Pakistan, kitschy and bombastic images are often sold as souvenirs at festivals and large social gatherings. After discovering them in 2021, photographer and National Geographic Explorer Matthieu Paley spent five years collecting these unique prints from different events and pilgrimages. Featuring fantastical depictions of actresses, soldiers, and fancy estates, the images are not about precision—they're about spectacle.

See more of these prints at the link in bio.

Photographs from Matthieu

The 1,847 islands of Raja Ampat, Indonesia, are home to more than 1,600 known species of fish, including manta rays, leopard sharks, and brown coral blennies. Thanks to the work of marine scientist Mark Erdmann, Indonesia banned commercial fishing and resource extraction across the islands around 20 years ago, designating much of the archipelago as a network of marine protected areas. Discover more about our one ocean at the link in bio.

Road collisions in Brazil have killed hundreds of giant anteaters and left many pups orphaned and in need of rehabilitation. At rehab centers, the young animals receive medical care as they regain their strength and are prepared for their possible reintroduction to the wild. National Geographic Explorer @fernando.faciole spent three years documenting these elusive mammals and the efforts underway to protect them.

Learn more about the threats giant anteaters face in Brazil at the link in bio.
